sections.content: You know *como* + indicative at the start of a sentence to give a cause from B1 Unit 32 (*Como no llegaste a tiempo, nos fuimos* = 'Since you didn't arrive on time, we left'), and *como* + present subjunctive as a **warning or threat** from B2 Unit 33 (*Como no entregues el informe hoy, perderemos el contrato* = 'If you don't hand in the report today, we'll lose the contract'). New here is the **present perfect subjunctive** after *como*, from B1 Unit 37, for something that may already have happened (*Como hayas tocado mi ordenador, tendremos un problema*), and how the structure sounds across the Spanish-speaking world. Notice that mood carries the entire distinction between cause (indicative) and warning (subjunctive). This structure is colloquial and especially common in Spain, though understood across the whole Spanish-speaking world; in Latin America, *si* + indicative (*Si no entregas el informe hoy…*) is more usual in everyday speech.

sections.title: Como + subjunctive (warning) vs como + indicative (cause)
rows: Warning or threat about the future (*Como te retrases, saldremos sin ti.*).
Warning about a recent action (*Como hayas olvidado la entrega, habrá problemas.*).
Stated cause or reason (*Como te retrasaste, salimos sin ti.*).
*Si* + indicative (*Si te retrasas, saldremos sin ti.*) — neutral everywhere.

items.spanish: Como no terminemos la entrega antes de las cinco, perderemos el contrato.
items.english: If we don't finish the delivery before five, we will lose the contract.

items.spanish: Como hayas dejado el informe sin revisar, tendremos que repetir todo.
items.english: If you've left the report unchecked, we'll have to redo everything.

items.spanish: Como no avisaste ayer, nadie estaba sobre aviso esta mañana.
items.english: Since you didn't let us know yesterday, nobody was forewarned this morning.

items.spanish: Tienes que llegar a tiempo; de lo contrario, no podremos contar contigo.
items.english: You have to arrive on time; otherwise, we won't be able to count on you.

sections.content: Always check the verb mood after *como*: indicative states a real cause ('since / because'), while present or perfect subjunctive turns *como* into a sharp warning ('if you dare…'). Never use the future or conditional directly after conditional *como*.
